claim: In insects and mammals, olfactory experience in early life alters olfactory behavior and function in later life.
source: In insects and mammals, olfactory experience in early life alters olfactory behavior and function in later life.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory plasticity that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In Drosophila, flies chronically exposed to a high concentration of a monomolecular odor exhibit reduced behavioral aversion to the familiar odor when it is reencountered.
source: In the vinegar fly Drosophila, flies chronically exposed to a high concentration of a monomolecular odor exhibit reduced behavioral aversion to the familiar odor when it is reencountered.
evidence: This statement references prior work in the field, as indicated by the context and subsequent citations in the manuscript.

claim: The change in olfactory behavior after chronic odor exposure has been attributed to selective decreases in the sensitivity of second-order olfactory projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe that respond to the overrepresented odor.
source: This change in olfactory behavior has been attributed to selective decreases in the sensitivity of second-order olfactory projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe that respond to the overrepresented odor.
evidence: This claim references prior interpretations in the literature about the mechanism of behavioral plasticity.

claim: Chronic exposure to three odors at naturally occurring concentrations did not result in decreased PN sensitivity but rather mildly increased responses to weak stimuli in most PN types.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that chronic exposure to three such odors did not result in decreased PN sensitivity but rather mildly increased responses to weak stimuli in most PN types.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Odor-evoked PN activity in response to stronger stimuli was mostly unaffected by odor experience.
source: Odor-evoked PN activity in response to stronger stimuli was mostly unaffected by odor experience.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: When present, plasticity was observed broadly in multiple PN types and thus was not selective for PNs receiving direct input from the chronically active ORNs.
source: When present, plasticity was observed broadly in multiple PN types and thus was not selective for PNs receiving direct input from the chronically active ORNs.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by experimental data comparing PNs receiving direct versus indirect input, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Chronic odor-mediated excitation of DL5 input ORNs did not affect PN intrinsic properties.
source: We further investigated the DL5 olfactory coding channel and found that chronic odor-mediated excitation of its input ORNs did not affect PN intrinsic properties, local inhibitory innervation, ORN responses or ORN-PN synaptic strength; however, broad-acting lateral excitation evoked by some odors was increased.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental measurements of input resistance and f-I curves shown in Figures 2F and 7A-C.

claim: Chronic odor-mediated excitation of DL5 input ORNs did not affect local inhibitory innervation.
source: We further investigated the DL5 olfactory coding channel and found that chronic odor-mediated excitation of its input ORNs did not affect PN intrinsic properties, local inhibitory innervation, ORN responses or ORN-PN synaptic strength; however, broad-acting lateral excitation evoked by some odors was increased.
evidence: This finding is supported by anatomical measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chronic odor-mediated excitation of DL5 input ORNs did not affect ORN responses.
source: We further investigated the DL5 olfactory coding channel and found that chronic odor-mediated excitation of its input ORNs did not affect PN intrinsic properties, local inhibitory innervation, ORN responses or ORN-PN synaptic strength; however, broad-acting lateral excitation evoked by some odors was increased.
evidence: This finding is supported by ORN recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: Chronic odor-mediated excitation of DL5 input ORNs did not affect ORN-PN synaptic strength.
source: We further investigated the DL5 olfactory coding channel and found that chronic odor-mediated excitation of its input ORNs did not affect PN intrinsic properties, local inhibitory innervation, ORN responses or ORN-PN synaptic strength; however, broad-acting lateral excitation evoked by some odors was increased.
evidence: This finding is supported by optogenetic measurements of unitary EPSCs shown in Figure 7D-G.

claim: Broad-acting lateral excitation evoked by some odors was increased after chronic odor exposure.
source: We further investigated the DL5 olfactory coding channel and found that chronic odor-mediated excitation of its input ORNs did not affect PN intrinsic properties, local inhibitory innervation, ORN responses or ORN-PN synaptic strength; however, broad-acting lateral excitation evoked by some odors was increased.
evidence: This finding is supported by measurements of lateral excitation in deafferented PNs shown in Figure 7H-J.

claim: PN odor coding is only mildly affected by strong persistent activation of a single olfactory input.
source: These results show that PN odor coding is only mildly affected by strong persistent activation of a single olfactory input, highlighting the stability of early stages of insect olfactory processing to significant perturbations in the sensory environment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Early stages of insect olfactory processing are stable to significant perturbations in the sensory environment.
source: These results show that PN odor coding is only mildly affected by strong persistent activation of a single olfactory input, highlighting the stability of early stages of insect olfactory processing to significant perturbations in the sensory environment.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Visual experience is required for the normal development of the mammalian visual system.
source: For example, visual experience is required for the normal development of the mammalian visual system (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: An important function of sensory plasticity is to adapt circuit function to the current statistical distribution of sensory inputs in the environment, allowing for more efficient sensory codes.
source: One prominent hypothesis is that an important function of sensory plasticity is to adapt circuit function to the current statistical distribution of sensory inputs in the environment, allowing for more efficient sensory codes (Barlow, 1961; Fiser et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2009; Pienkowski and Eggermont, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: The efficient coding hypothesis requires sensory driven plasticity to be stimulus- and cell-specific.
source: This hypothesis requires sensory driven plasticity to be stimulus- and cell-specific; in other words, neurons encoding specific stimuli that occur very frequently (or very rarely) in the environment should be selectively affected by plasticity (Das et al., 2011; Kreile et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Sengpiel et al., 1999; Wilson et al., 1985; Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the efficient coding hypothesis, supported by citations.

claim: Each glomerulus receives direct input from only a single class of primary olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), all expressing the same olfactory receptor.
source: Each glomerulus receives direct input from only a single class of primary olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), all expressing the same olfactory receptor, and, thus, all sensitive to the same chemical feature(s) (Ressler et al., 1994; Vassar et al., 1994; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Vosshall et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact about olfactory system organization, supported by citations.

claim: The dendrites of each second-order uniglomerular projection neuron (PN) arborize in only a single glomerulus.
source: Furthermore, the dendrites of each second-order uniglomerular projection neuron (PN) arborize in only a single glomerulus, so each PN receives direct input from only a single class of ORNs (Stocker et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact supported by citation.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the majority of odorant receptors and ORN subtypes have been mapped to their corresponding glomeruli in the brain.
source: In the vinegar fly Drosophila melanogaster, the majority of odorant receptors and ORN subtypes have been mapped to their corresponding glomeruli in the brain (Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Silbering et al., 2011), and the odor tuning profiles for a large subset of the odorant receptors have been characterized (Silbering et al., 2011; de Bruyne et al., 1999; de Bruyne et al., 2001; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Hallem et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior mapping studies.

claim: Specific odors can be used to selectively target neural activation of defined olfactory channels in Drosophila.
source: As a result, specific odors can be used to selectively target neural activation of defined olfactory channels (Olsen et al., 2010; Schlief and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This capability is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Passive odor experience in early life can alter olfactory circuit structure and function, including olfactory preference or discrimination ability.
source: Passive odor experience in early life, in the absence of explicit coupling to reward or punishment, can alter olfactory circuit structure and function, including olfactory preference or discrimination ability (Mandairon and Linster, 2009; Mandairon et al., 2006a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chronic odor exposure in rodents can trigger changes in the structural connectivity and physiological response properties of neurons in the olfactory bulb.
source: For instance, chronic odor exposure in rodents can trigger changes in the structural connectivity and physiological response properties of neurons in the olfactory bulb, the first central processing area for odors in the brain (Wilson et al., 1985; Liu and Urban, 2017; Liu et al., 2016; Todrank et al., 2011; Woo et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in rodents.

claim: In insects, passive odor experience has been found to impact olfactory processing in the antennal lobe.
source: In insects, passive odor experience has also been found to impact olfactory processing in the antennal lobe, the insect analog of the olfactory bulb (Golovin and Broadie, 2016; Twick et al., 2014; Bai and Suzuki, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in insects.

claim: Chronic exposure to high concentrations of monomolecular odor reduces behavioral avoidance toward the familiar odor selectively when it is reencountered.
source: Chronic exposure to high concentrations of monomolecular odor, stimuli which are typically strongly aversive, reduces behavioral avoidance toward the familiar odor selectively when it is reencountered (Das et al., 2011; Devaud et al., 2001; Devaud et al., 2003); in parallel, structural alterations in glomerular volume are also observed (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Devaud et al., 2001; Devaud et al., 2003; Golovin et al., 2019; Kidd et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Structural alterations in glomerular volume are observed in parallel with reduced behavioral avoidance after chronic odor exposure.
source: Chronic exposure to high concentrations of monomolecular odor, stimuli which are typically strongly aversive, reduces behavioral avoidance toward the familiar odor selectively when it is reencountered (Das et al., 2011; Devaud et al., 2001; Devaud et al., 2003); in parallel, structural alterations in glomerular volume are also observed (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Devaud et al., 2001; Devaud et al., 2003; Golovin et al., 2019; Kidd et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Odor experience-dependent reductions in olfactory aversion have been interpreted as a form of long-term behavioral habituation to overrepresented stimuli in the environment.
source: Odor experience-dependent reductions in olfactory aversion have been interpreted as a form of long-term behavioral habituation to overrepresented stimuli in the environment and are attributed to reduced PN responses in flies chronically exposed to odor (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; see also Kidd et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation from prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: Behavioral plasticity after chronic odor exposure is odor-specific and does not generalize to other odors.
source: Importantly, since behavioral plasticity is odor-specific and does not generalize to other odors, structural and functional neural plasticity are also believed to be glomerulus-specific (and thus odor-specific), acting to selectively reduce the olfactory sensitivity of only those PNs activated by the overrepresented stimuli.
evidence: This statement references prior findings about the specificity of behavioral plasticity.

claim: Past studies exposed animals to intense monomolecular odors which typically excite many classes of ORN inputs.
source: However, since past studies exposed animals to intense monomolecular odors (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Devaud et al., 2001; Devaud et al., 2003; Golovin et al., 2019; Chodankar et al., 2020; e.g. from odor sources of 10% isoamyl acetate [v/v] or 20% ethyl butyrate [v/v]), which typically excite many classes of ORN inputs, stringent testing of this idea has not been possible.
evidence: This is a critique of prior experimental approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Nearly all studies use very high concentrations of monomolecular odorants during the exposure period, at intensities that are not encountered in the natural world.
source: Finally, nearly all studies, in insects or in mammals, use very high concentrations of monomolecular odorants during the exposure period, at intensities that are not encountered in the natural world (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a critique of prior experimental approaches based on knowledge of natural odor concentrations.

claim: The odor stimulus amplitude changed less than 20% over 12 hours during chronic exposure.
source: Photoionization measurements of the odor concentration in the rearing bottle demonstrated that the stimulus amplitude changed <20% over 12 hr (Figure 1B), after which the odor source was refreshed.
evidence: This measurement is supported by photoionization detector data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The largest decrease in delivered odor concentration occurred within the first 2 hours and slowed significantly thereafter.
source: The largest decrease in delivered odor concentration occurred within the first 2 hr and slowed significantly thereafter.
evidence: This observation is based on the photoionization measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At a 20-second interstimulus interval, the odors reliably activated cognate PNs to saturating or near saturating firing rates over many trials.
source: Pilot recordings showed that, at this interstimulus interval, the odors reliably activated cognate PNs to saturating or near saturating firing rates over many trials (Figure 1C–D, and data not shown; see also Figure 2Q).
evidence: This finding is supported by pilot electrophysiology data shown in Figures 1C-D and 2Q.

claim: PN response duration to the 1 s stimulus increased modestly with successive odor presentations.
source: In addition, PN response duration to the 1 s stimulus increased modestly with successive odor presentations.
evidence: This observation is based on pilot recordings, as indicated by the context.

claim: The odor exposure protocol more than doubled the average firing rate of the targeted PN and elicited more than a million extra spikes in the activated PN over the course of the 2-day period of exposure.
source: On average, this odor exposure protocol more than doubled the average firing rate of the targeted PN and elicited more than a million extra spikes in the activated PN over the course of the 2-day period of exposure (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental protocol and PN firing rates.

claim: Low concentrations of E2-hexenal (10–10–10–9) elicited increased levels of odor-evoked membrane depolarization in DL5 PNs from E2-hexenal exposed flies compared to solvent-exposed flies.
source: However, low concentrations of E2-hexenal (10–10–10–9) elicited increased levels of odor-evoked membrane depolarization in DL5 PNs from E2-hexenal exposed flies compared to solvent-exposed flies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DL5 PN responses elicited by moderate to high concentrations of E2-hexenal (>10–8) were unchanged in E2-hexenal exposed flies, as compared to controls.
source: DL5 PN responses elicited by moderate to high concentrations of E2-hexenal (>10–8) were unchanged in E2-hexenal exposed flies, as compared to controls (Figure 2B and Q).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 2B and 2Q.

claim: E2-hexenal exposure increased odor-evoked firing rates in DL5 PNs to weak but not strong levels of stimulation.
source: This statistical analysis confirmed that E2-hexenal exposure increased odor-evoked firing rates in DL5 PNs to weak but not strong levels of stimulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: VM7 PNs in 2-butanone-exposed flies exhibited modest increases in odor-evoked depolarization in response to direct stimulation as compared to control flies, with effects more pronounced at weak concentrations.
source: Like the DL5 glomerulus, VM7 PNs in 2-butanone-exposed flies exhibited modest increases in odor-evoked depolarization in response to direct stimulation (by 2-butanone) as compared to control flies, and these effects were more pronounced at weak concentrations (10–7; Figure 2H–I and R).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 2H-I and 2R.

claim: Chronic activation of direct ORN input to VA6 PNs by exposure to geranyl acetate did not alter PN odor responses across the entire range of concentrations tested.
source: However, chronic activation of direct ORN input to VA6 PNs by exposure to geranyl acetate did not alter PN odor responses across the entire range of concentrations of the familiar odor geranyl acetate, neither at the level of membrane depolarization nor firing rate (Figure 2L–P and S).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 2L-P and 2S.

claim: Chronic indirect excitation evoked plasticity with varying properties in different PNs.
source: Chronic indirect excitation evoked plasticity with varying properties in different PNs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on experimental data comparing different PN types.

claim: In E2-hexenal exposed flies, non-DL5 PNs had mildly enhanced responses to weak stimuli.
source: In E2-hexenal exposed flies, non-DL5 PNs had mildly enhanced responses to weak stimuli (Figure 3B and J).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 3B and 3J.

claim: Odor-evoked depolarization in VM7 PNs from E2-hexenal-exposed flies had a more pronounced and prolonged after hyperpolarization as compared to controls.
source: For example, odor-evoked depolarization in VM7 PNs from E2-hexenal-exposed flies had a more pronounced and prolonged after hyperpolarization as compared to controls (Figure 3B and E), or as compared to flies that experienced chronic direct excitation (2-butanone exposed; Figures 2H and 3F).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 3B, 3E, 2H, and 3F.

claim: In recordings from VA6 PNs in E2-hexenal exposed flies, post-stimulus excitation was enhanced across multiple odor concentrations, as compared to solvent-exposed controls.
source: In recordings from VA6 PNs in E2-hexenal exposed flies, this post-stimulus excitation was enhanced across multiple odor concentrations, as compared to solvent-exposed controls (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 3J-K.

claim: Chronic, focal excitation of a single ORN class can lead to changes in PN odor response properties in multiple glomeruli, including in glomeruli not receiving direct synaptic input from the chronically activated ORN class.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrated that chronic, focal excitation of a single ORN class can lead to changes in PN odor response properties in multiple glomeruli, including in glomeruli not receiving direct synaptic input from the chronically activated ORN class.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Chronic, sustained exposure to 20% geranyl acetate had little or no effect on VA6 PN odor responses spanning the range of concentrations of geranyl acetate tested.
source: We found that chronic, sustained exposure to 20% geranyl acetate had little or no effect on VA6 PN odor responses spanning the range of concentrations of geranyl acetate tested (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 4B-F.

claim: Odor responses in DM6 PNs were moderately increased in 20% geranyl acetate-exposed flies as compared to solvent-exposed control flies.
source: Odor responses in DM6 PNs, which are excited by valeric acid, were moderately increased in 20% geranyl acetate-exposed flies as compared to solvent-exposed control flies (Figure 4H–L).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 4H-L.

claim: Uninterrupted, chronic exposure to an intense monomolecular odor, 20% geranyl acetate, for 4 days has only a moderate effect on PN odor coding, qualitatively similar to the impact of long-lasting but intermittent exposure to odors at lower, naturalistic concentrations.
source: These results indicate that uninterrupted, chronic exposure to an intense monomolecular odor, 20% geranyl acetate, for 4 days has only a moderate effect on PN odor coding, qualitatively similar to the impact of long-lasting but intermittent exposure to odors at lower, naturalistic concentrations (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on data from Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Reductions in PN olfactory sensitivity were not observed in flies reared in any of the four odorized environments studied.
source: We did not observe reductions in PN olfactory sensitivity in flies reared in any of the four odorized environments we studied.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Blending pentyl acetate with 2-butanone reduced VM7 PN responses, as compared to their response to 2-butanone alone.
source: Overall, blending pentyl acetate with 2-butanone reduced VM7 PN responses, as compared to their response to 2-butanone alone (Figures 5B and 2H and Figures 5E and 3B).
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison of electrophysiology data shown in Figures 5B, 2H, 5E, and 3B.

claim: Such mixture inhibition is well understood to be a consequence of lateral GABAergic inhibition elicited by activity in non-VM7 ORNs.
source: Such mixture inhibition is well understood to be a consequence of lateral GABAergic inhibition elicited by activity in non-VM7 ORNs (Olsen et al., 2010; Olsen and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: VM7 responses to mixed direct and indirect input (driven by blends of 2-butanone and pentyl acetate) were similar in control and 2-butanone exposed flies.
source: Whereas responses of VM7 PNs to direct excitation (driven by 2-butanone) were modestly enhanced in 2-butanone exposed flies (Figure 2H–I), VM7 responses to mixed direct and indirect input (driven by blends of 2-butanone and pentyl acetate) were similar in control and 2-butanone exposed flies (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison of data in Figures 2H-I and 5B-C.

claim: VM7 PN responses to odor mixtures of 2-butanone and pentyl acetate were indistinguishable between E2-hexenal and solvent-exposed flies.
source: Whereas chronic exposure to E2-hexenal altered VM7 PN responses to 2-butanone (Figure 3B–C and E), VM7 PN responses to odor mixtures of 2-butanone and pentyl acetate were indistinguishable between E2-hexenal and solvent-exposed flies (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison of data in Figures 3B-C, 3E, and 5E-F.

claim: Lateral inhibition may be impacted by chronic odor exposure, such that odor-evoked input elicits more inhibition to counter modest increases in PN excitation.
source: These observations suggest that lateral inhibition may also be impacted by chronic odor exposure, such that odor-evoked input elicits more inhibition to counter modest increases in PN excitation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the mixture response data.

claim: Levels of innervation of individual olfactory glomeruli by the neurites of large subpopulations of inhibitory LNs were largely unchanged by chronic odor exposure.
source: Levels of innervation of individual olfactory glomeruli by the neurites of large subpopulations of inhibitory LNs (iLNs; measured as the ratio of iLN neurites to total synaptic neuropil) were largely unchanged by chronic odor exposure (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This finding is supported by anatomical measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: In flies chronically exposed to E2-hexenal only, many glomeruli tended to be smaller in volume than their counterparts in solvent-exposed flies.
source: Unexpectedly, in flies chronically exposed to E2-hexenal only, many glomeruli tended to be smaller in volume than their counterparts in solvent-exposed flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, G).
evidence: This finding is supported by anatomical measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and G.

claim: Similar trends in glomerular volume were not observed in parallel experiments where flies were chronically exposed to 2-butanone.
source: Similar trends, however, were not observed in parallel experiments where flies were chronically exposed to 2-butanone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This finding is supported by anatomical measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Chronic exposure to some, but not all, odors can elicit mild anatomical perturbations in the olfactory circuit.
source: Thus, chronic exposure to some, but not all, odors can elicit mild anatomical perturbations in the olfactory circuit.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the anatomical data from Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under the odor exposure conditions used in this study, changes in glomerular volume were not glomerulus-specific but extended globally beyond the chronically active glomerulus.
source: In contrast with previous reports (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Devaud et al., 2001), however, under our odor exposure conditions, changes in glomerular volume were not glomerulus-specific but extended globally beyond the chronically active glomerulus.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the anatomical data and contrasts with prior reports.

claim: Prior studies have suggested that chronic odor exposure increases the sensitivity of ORNs.
source: Prior studies have suggested that chronic odor exposure increases the sensitivity of ORNs (Chakraborty et al., 2009; Iyengar et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement references prior findings in the literature.

claim: Chronic activation of ab4a ORNs in E2-hexenal exposed flies did not significantly impact spontaneous or odor-evoked firing rates across a wide range of stimulus concentrations.
source: We observed that chronic activation of either ORN type – ab4a ORNs in E2-hexenal exposed flies or pb1a ORNs in 2-butanone exposed flies – did not significantly impact spontaneous (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G) or odor-evoked firing rates across a wide range of stimulus concentrations (Figure 6B–C and E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), including those lower concentrations which elicited enhanced responses in postsynaptic DL5 or VM7 PNs (Figure 2B–E and H–I).
evidence: This finding is supported by single-sensillum recording data shown in Figures 6B-C, 6E-F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chronic activation of pb1a ORNs in 2-butanone exposed flies did not significantly impact spontaneous or odor-evoked firing rates across a wide range of stimulus concentrations.
source: We observed that chronic activation of either ORN type – ab4a ORNs in E2-hexenal exposed flies or pb1a ORNs in 2-butanone exposed flies – did not significantly impact spontaneous (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G) or odor-evoked firing rates across a wide range of stimulus concentrations (Figure 6B–C and E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), including those lower concentrations which elicited enhanced responses in postsynaptic DL5 or VM7 PNs (Figure 2B–E and H–I).
evidence: This finding is supported by single-sensillum recording data shown in Figures 6B-C, 6E-F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: pb1a ORN responses were largely unaffected by E2-hexenal exposure.
source: These experiments showed that pb1a odor responses were largely unaffected by E2-hexenal exposure (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This finding is supported by single-sensillum recording data shown in Figures 6H-I.

claim: Functional imaging showed that odor-evoked responses in ab4a ORN terminals in glomerulus DL5 were indistinguishable between E2-hexenal exposed and control flies across the entire range of odor concentrations tested.
source: However, functional imaging showed that odor-evoked responses in ab4a ORN terminals in glomerulus DL5 were indistinguishable between E2-hexenal exposed and control flies across the entire range of odor concentrations tested (Figure 6L–M, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This finding is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 6L-M and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ORN odor responses are unaffected by perturbations in the odor environment that drive over a million additional spikes in each ORN over the course of 2 days of exposure.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that ORN odor responses are unaffected by perturbations in the odor environment that drive over a million additional spikes in each ORN over the course of 2 days of exposure.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ORN recording and imaging data from Figure 6.

claim: The PN plasticity observed likely stems from central cellular or circuit mechanisms, rather than from changes at the periphery.
source: They also imply that the PN plasticity we observe likely stems from central cellular or circuit mechanisms, rather than from changes at the periphery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that ORN responses are unchanged.

claim: Postsynaptic input resistance was unaltered by chronic exposure to any of the odors in the study.
source: Comparisons of the input resistance of PNs recorded in odor-exposed and control flies showed that postsynaptic input resistance was unaltered by chronic exposure to any of the odors in our study, regardless of odor concentration or whether PNs received direct or indirect chronic activation (Figures 2F, J, P—4F and L).
evidence: This finding is supported by input resistance measurements shown in Figures 2F, 2J, 2P, 4F, and 4L.

claim: f-I curves directly measuring the firing rate of deafferented DL5 PNs in response to current injection at the soma were indistinguishable between control and E2-hexenal exposed flies.
source: Consistent with these observations, f-I curves directly measuring the firing rate of deafferented DL5 PNs in response to current injection at the soma (Figure 7A) were indistinguishable between control and E2-hexenal exposed flies (Figure 7B–C; see also Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiology data from deafferented PNs shown in Figures 7A-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The intrinsic excitability of PNs is unaltered by chronic odor exposure and does not account for the increase in PN sensitivity to weak odors.
source: These results indicate that the intrinsic excitability of PNs is unaltered by chronic odor exposure and does not account for the increase in PN sensitivity to weak odors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the input resistance and f-I curve measurements.

claim: Average DL5 uEPSC amplitudes and response kinetics were indistinguishable between solvent and E2-hexenal exposed flies.
source: Average DL5 uEPSC amplitudes and response kinetics were indistinguishable between solvent and E2-hexenal exposed flies (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This finding is supported by optogenetic measurements shown in Figures 7F-G.

claim: ORN-PN strength is unchanged by chronic odor exposure and is unlikely to account for enhanced DL5 PN responses to weak stimuli in E2-hexenal exposed flies.
source: This result shows that ORN-PN strength is unchanged by chronic odor exposure and is unlikely to account for enhanced DL5 PN responses to weak stimuli in E2-hexenal exposed flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the uEPSC measurements.

claim: Many, but not all, odors evoked increased lateral excitation in VA6 PNs from E2-hexenal exposed flies, as compared to solvent-exposed flies.
source: Many, but not all, odors evoked increased lateral excitation in VA6 PNs from E2-hexenal exposed flies, as compared to solvent-exposed flies (Figure 7I–J).
evidence: This finding is supported by measurements from deafferented PNs shown in Figures 7I-J.

claim: The average amount of odor-evoked lateral excitation across all stimuli was increased in E2-hexenal exposed flies, as compared to solvent-exposed controls.
source: This analysis confirmed that the average amount of odor-evoked lateral excitation across all stimuli was increased in E2-hexenal exposed flies, as compared to solvent-exposed controls (Figure 7J).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of lateral excitation measurements shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Chronic odor exposure increases the overall strength of global excitatory coupling among glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: These results suggest that chronic odor exposure increases the overall strength of global excitatory coupling among glomeruli in the antennal lobe after chronic odor exposure, which may contribute to the heightened sensitivity of PNs to weak odors.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the lateral excitation measurements.

claim: Strong, persistent activation of a single class of ORNs triggers only limited plasticity at early stages of olfactory processing in Drosophila.
source: We found that strong, persistent activation of a single class of ORNs triggers only limited plasticity at early stages of olfactory processing in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study based on all experimental findings.

claim: Chronic exposure to monomolecular odors at concentrations that can be found in the natural world elicited modest increases in the olfactory sensitivity of some PNs.
source: Chronic exposure to monomolecular odors at concentrations that can be found in the natural world elicited modest increases in the olfactory sensitivity of some PNs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings from Figures 2-4.

claim: Qualitatively similar effects on PN odor coding were observed even when exposing flies to high concentrations of a monomolecular odor, geranyl acetate.
source: Qualitatively similar effects on PN odor coding were observed even when exposing flies to high concentrations of a monomolecular odor, geranyl acetate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on comparison of data from Figures 2-3 and Figure 4.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity in PNs mostly affected the encoding of weak odor stimuli, whereas responses to stronger odors were largely unaffected.
source: When present, experience-dependent plasticity in PNs mostly affected the encoding of weak odor stimuli, whereas responses to stronger odors, which more strongly recruit local inhibition, were largely unaffected.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the concentration-response data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Many elements of the antennal lobe circuit, including ORN sensitivity, PN intrinsic properties, and ORN-PN synapse strength, were unaffected by chronic ORN activation.
source: Many elements of the antennal lobe circuit, including ORN sensitivity, PN intrinsic properties, and ORN-PN synapse strength, were unaffected by chronic ORN activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Figures 2, 6, and 7.

claim: Plasticity triggered by chronic ORN activity was observed not only in PNs corresponding to the glomerulus that receives direct input from the chronically active ORNs but also in PNs corresponding to other glomeruli.
source: Plasticity triggered by chronic ORN activity was observed not only in PNs corresponding to the glomerulus that receives direct input from the chronically active ORNs but also in PNs corresponding to other glomeruli, indicating that experience-dependent plasticity in PNs is not glomerulus- or odor-specific.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on comparison of data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity in PNs is not glomerulus- or odor-specific.
source: Plasticity triggered by chronic ORN activity was observed not only in PNs corresponding to the glomerulus that receives direct input from the chronically active ORNs but also in PNs corresponding to other glomeruli, indicating that experience-dependent plasticity in PNs is not glomerulus- or odor-specific.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Odor exposure can boost the level of lateral excitatory coupling between some PNs.
source: This result implicates lateral interactions between glomeruli as having a role in olfactory plasticity, consistent with our observation that odor exposure can boost the level of lateral excitatory coupling between some PNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lateral excitation measurements in Figure 7.

claim: Even in odor environments that elicit unusually high, long-lasting levels of activity in a single ORN class, the representation of odors in the antennal lobe is mostly stable.
source: Thus, even in odor environments that elicit unusually high, long-lasting levels of activity in a single ORN class, the representation of odors in the antennal lobe is mostly stable.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental findings.

claim: Chronic odor stimulation results in either no or mild changes in PN responses, which sensitize PNs to weak stimuli and extend the lower range of stimulus intensities dynamically encoded by the PN.
source: Chronic odor stimulation results in either no or mild changes in PN responses, which sensitize PNs to weak stimuli and extend the lower range of stimulus intensities dynamically encoded by the PN.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Reduced PN responses were not observed in response to chronic excitation in any condition tested.
source: Reduced PN responses were not observed in response to chronic excitation in any condition we tested, inconsistent with the hypothesis that PN olfactory codes adjust to the frequency with which specific odors are encountered in the environment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data.

claim: The results are inconsistent with the hypothesis that PN olfactory codes adjust to the frequency with which specific odors are encountered in the environment.
source: Reduced PN responses were not observed in response to chronic excitation in any condition we tested, inconsistent with the hypothesis that PN olfactory codes adjust to the frequency with which specific odors are encountered in the environment.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Prior studies in flies found that chronic exposure to monomolecular odors delivered at high concentrations selectively reduced the sensitivity of PNs activated by these odors.
source: These results contrast with prior studies in flies in which chronic exposure to monomolecular odors delivered at high concentrations selectively reduced the sensitivity of PNs activated by these odors (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement references prior findings in the literature.

claim: A prior study observed that sustained, chronic exposure of flies to 1% geranyl acetate weakly enhanced VA6 PN responses.
source: A prior study observed that sustained, chronic exposure of flies to 1% geranyl acetate weakly enhanced VA6 PN responses (Kidd et al., 2015), a result which the current study confirms and extends to additional odors and glomeruli.
evidence: This statement references a prior finding and indicates the current study confirms it.

claim: A study in mice found that odor-evoked mitral cell activity in the olfactory bulb was modestly increased after chronic odor exposure to intense monomolecular odors.
source: Another analogous study in mice found that odor-evoked mitral cell activity in the olfactory bulb was modestly increased after chronic odor exposure to intense monomolecular odors (Liu and Urban, 2017).
evidence: This statement references a prior finding in mice.

claim: Flies were exposed to periodic 1 s pulses of odor at estimated concentrations of approximately 10 ppb to approximately 10 ppm in air.
source: In this study, flies were exposed to periodic 1 s pulses of odor at estimated concentrations of ~10 ppb to ~10 ppm in air (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Nearly all prior studies investigating olfactory plasticity chronically excite the olfactory system using odors delivered at concentrations ranging from approximately 10^3 to approximately 10^5 ppm in air.
source: Nearly all prior studies investigating olfactory plasticity, in flies or rodents, chronically excite the olfactory system using odors delivered at comparatively higher concentrations, generally ranging from ~103 to ~105 ppm in air (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Liu and Urban, 2017; Devaud et al., 2001; Chodankar et al., 2020; Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement characterizes prior experimental approaches with citations.

claim: Headspace concentrations of the most abundant small ester, alcohol, and aldehyde volatiles common in fruit odor sources typically range from approximately 1 ppb to approximately 10 ppm in air.
source: Such stimuli are unlikely to be found in natural odor sources; for comparison, headspace concentrations of the most abundant small ester, alcohol, and aldehyde volatiles common in fruit odor sources typically range from ~1 ppb to ~10 ppm in air (e.g. see Boschetti et al., 1999; Farneti et al., 2017; Jordán et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement provides context about natural odor concentrations, supported by citations.

claim: For many volatile organic compounds, prolonged exposure at concentrations that exceed approximately 10^3 ppm is considered hazardous to human life or health.
source: Indeed, for many volatile organic compounds, prolonged exposure at concentrations that exceed ~103 ppm is considered hazardous to human life or health (NIOSH CDC, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to occupational health standards.

claim: Some prior studies showed that the effects of chronic odor exposure on olfactory neuron responses and anatomical volume affect only specific glomeruli, although the direction of these effects varied between studies.
source: Some prior studies showed that the effects of chronic odor exposure on olfactory neuron responses and anatomical volume affect only specific glomeruli, although the direction of these effects varied between studies (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Devaud et al., 2001; Devaud et al., 2003; Chakraborty et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement summarizes prior findings with citations.

claim: Chronic olfactory stimulation broadly affects many PN types, similar to findings in mouse where chronic odor exposure induced widespread, global enhancement of mitral cell excitability across the olfactory bulb.
source: Our observation that chronic olfactory stimulation broadly affects many PN types is similar to that of a recent functional imaging study in mouse which found that chronic odor exposure in early postnatal life induced widespread, global enhancement of mitral cell excitability across the olfactory bulb (Liu and Urban, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative statement linking the current findings to prior work in mice.

claim: Chronic, persistent olfactory activity may function to adjust the overall gain or sensitivity of the circuit, especially in the weak stimulus regime.
source: Chronic, persistent olfactory activity may function to adjust the overall gain or sensitivity of the circuit, especially in the weak stimulus regime.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Widespread increase in excitability might reflect a form of generalized sensory enrichment that has been previously described in mammalian olfactory, visual, and auditory systems.
source: Such a widespread increase in excitability might reflect a form of generalized sensory enrichment that has been previously described in mammalian olfactory (Mandairon et al., 2006b; Rochefort et al., 2002), visual (Beaulieu and Cynader, 1990), and auditory (Engineer et al., 2004) systems.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking the findings to prior concepts in sensory neuroscience.

claim: Past studies in insects have implicated local inhibitory networks in mediating short- and long-timescale plasticity in the antennal lobe.
source: Indeed, past studies in insects have implicated local inhibitory networks in mediating short- and long-timescale plasticity in the antennal lobe.
evidence: This statement references prior work on circuit mechanisms of plasticity.

claim: Repeated encounters with a given odor over short timescales (seconds to minutes) restructures PN activity to increase the reliability of PN representations of the odor.
source: For instance, repeated encounters with a given odor over short timescales (seconds to minutes) restructures PN activity to increase the reliability of PN representations of the odor (Stopfer and Laurent, 1999; Franco and Yaksi, 2021; computational models indicate this plasticity can be explained by facilitation of inhibitory connections in the antennal lobe; Bazhenov et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement references prior findings about short-term plasticity.

claim: In plasticity elicited by odor experience on long timescales (days), past work suggests glomerulus-specific plasticity is mediated by the strengthening of inputs from specific genetically defined subsets of iLNs.
source: In plasticity elicited by odor experience on long timescales (days), past work suggests glomerulus-specific plasticity is mediated by the strengthening of inputs from specific genetically defined subsets of iLNs (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Golovin and Broadie, 2016).
evidence: This statement references prior hypotheses about long-term plasticity mechanisms.

claim: The observation that olfactory plasticity is not necessarily glomerulus-specific is consistent with the broadly innervating anatomical characteristics of both excitatory and iLNs.
source: Our observation that olfactory plasticity is not necessarily glomerulus-specific is consistent with the broadly innervating anatomical characteristics of both excitatory and iLNs.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to known anatomy.

claim: Prior work in fly found that chronic exposure to esters increased the sensitivity of ORNs to these odors.
source: Prior work in fly found that chronic exposure to esters increased the sensitivity of ORNs to these odors (Chakraborty et al., 2009; Iyengar et al., 2010), and multiple studies in rodents have concluded that chronic odor exposure evokes plasticity in ORN responses (Wang et al., 1993; Cadiou et al., 2014; Cavallin et al., 2010; Kass et al., 2013; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Watt et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement references prior findings about ORN plasticity.

claim: Multiple studies in rodents have concluded that chronic odor exposure evokes plasticity in ORN responses.
source: Prior work in fly found that chronic exposure to esters increased the sensitivity of ORNs to these odors (Chakraborty et al., 2009; Iyengar et al., 2010), and multiple studies in rodents have concluded that chronic odor exposure evokes plasticity in ORN responses (Wang et al., 1993; Cadiou et al., 2014; Cavallin et al., 2010; Kass et al., 2013; Santoro and Dulac, 2012; Watt et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement references prior findings about ORN plasticity in rodents.

claim: A change in the strength of lateral excitatory coupling between eLNs and PNs has been previously implicated in the slow recovery of odor responses in chronically deafferented PNs.
source: A change in the strength of lateral excitatory coupling between eLNs and PNs has also been previously implicated in the slow recovery of odor responses in chronically deafferented PNs (Kazama et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement references a prior finding about lateral excitation in a different context.

claim: The lateral excitatory network might serve as a substrate for olfactory plasticity in multiple contexts.
source: Thus, the lateral excitatory network might serve as a substrate for olfactory plasticity in multiple contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the current findings and prior work.

claim: Many studies in insect and in mammals have demonstrated that prior experience with an odor impacts how an animal subsequently responds to it.
source: Many studies in insect and in mammals have demonstrated that prior experience with an odor impacts how an animal subsequently responds to it.
evidence: This is a general statement about behavioral plasticity based on established knowledge.

claim: Reports of reduced PN responses to overrepresented odors in the environment were central to the interpretation of reduced behavioral aversion of flies toward familiar odors as a form of behavioral habituation.
source: Reports of reduced PN responses to overrepresented odors in the environment (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007) were central to the interpretation of reduced behavioral aversion of flies toward familiar odors as a form of behavioral habituation.
evidence: This statement references prior interpretations in the literature.

claim: Nearly all studies use high concentrations of monomolecular odor (from a approximately 1-20% v/v source), which are nearly always aversive to animals.
source: However, since nearly all studies use high concentrations of monomolecular odor (from a ~1–20% v/v source), which are nearly always aversive to animals, these experiments do not disambiguate whether reduced behavioral aversion reflects behavioral habituation to an aversive odor or increased attraction (or tolerance) to an aversive odor.
evidence: This is a critique of prior experimental designs.

claim: In one study where flies were chronically exposed to monomolecular odors at lower concentrations (approximately 0.01-1%) that are attractive to flies, odor experience increased behavioral attraction toward the familiar odor.
source: In one study where flies were chronically exposed to monomolecular odors at lower concentrations (~0.01–1%) that are attractive to flies, odor experience increased behavioral attraction toward the familiar odor (Chakraborty et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement references a prior finding about behavioral plasticity.

claim: Other work from the authors' laboratory shows that chronic exposure of flies in early life to odors from natural sources increases behavioral attraction to these odors.
source: In agreement, other work from our laboratory shows that chronic exposure of flies in early life to odors from natural sources increases behavioral attraction to these odors (Dylla et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement references work from the same laboratory.

claim: Prior studies have suggested that experience-dependent modification of olfactory behavior in fly stems from odor-specific changes in the structure and function of the antennal lobe, which act to reduce PN sensitivity to frequent or abundant odors in the environment.
source: Prior studies have suggested that experience-dependent modification of olfactory behavior in fly stems from odor-specific changes in the structure and function of the antennal lobe, which act to reduce PN sensitivity to frequent or abundant odors in the environment (Das et al., 2011; Sachse et al., 2007; Devaud et al., 2001; Sudhakaran et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement references prior hypotheses in the literature.

claim: The overall stability of odor coding in PNs argues against the idea that experience-dependent modification of olfactory behavior stems from odor-specific changes in the antennal lobe that reduce PN sensitivity.
source: The overall stability of odor coding in PNs, the major output from the antennal lobe, in the face of significant perturbations in the odor environment that chronically alters the distribution of sensory input to the fly olfactory system, argues against this idea.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Given that most typical odors are broadly encoded across many glomeruli, glomerulus-selective plasticity in the antennal lobe would seem to be an inefficient substrate for odor-specific plasticity.
source: Indeed, given that most typical odors are broadly encoded across many glomeruli, glomerulus-selective plasticity in the antennal lobe would seem to be an inefficient substrate for odor-specific plasticity since most individual glomeruli participate in the representation of many different odors.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on knowledge of odor coding.

claim: If chronic exposure to odors in early life is reinterpreted as an increase in attraction or acceptance of familiar odors, the observation of stable PN responses suggests that the neural mechanism responsible for behavioral plasticity likely acts downstream of the antennal lobe.
source: If chronic exposure to odors in early life is reinterpreted as an increase in attraction or acceptance of familiar odors, rather than habituation toward them, our observation of stable PN responses in odor-exposed flies suggests that the neural mechanism responsible for behavioral plasticity likely acts downstream of the antennal lobe.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The mushroom body has been extensively studied for its role in associative learning.
source: One higher order olfactory area which receives antennal lobe output, the mushroom body, has been extensively studied for its role in associative learning (Heisenberg, 2003).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about the mushroom body.

claim: Chronic odor exposure experiments are nearly always carried out in the presence of food, which may signal to flies a positive value of the environment and become associated with the odor.
source: Indeed, chronic odor exposure experiments are nearly always, by necessity, carried out in the presence of food, which may signal to flies a positive value of the environment and become associated with the odor.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential confounds in chronic odor exposure experiments.

claim: The stability of odor responses in early olfactory processing areas, even when challenged with persistent perturbations in the sensory environment, may reflect a more general design principle of sensory circuits.
source: The stability of odor responses in early olfactory processing areas, even when challenged with persistent perturbations in the sensory environment, may reflect a more general design principle of sensory circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation placing the findings in a broader context.

claim: In mammalian nervous systems, the function of early stages of sensory processing closer to the periphery is less dependent on normal sensory experience than later stages of cortical processing.
source: Even in mammalian nervous systems, which exhibit an overall higher degree of neural plasticity than insect systems, the function of early stages of sensory processing closer to the periphery is less dependent on normal sensory experience than later stages of cortical processing.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about sensory system organization.

claim: Normal visual experience is required for normal topographic maps, orientation selectivity, and direction selectivity in higher visual areas.
source: For example, although normal visual experience is required for normal topographic maps, orientation selectivity, and direction selectivity in higher visual areas (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Huberman et al., 2008), the structure and function of retinal circuitry are much less impacted by abnormal visual experience (D'Orazi et al., 2014; Elstrott and Feller, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in visual neuroscience.

claim: The structure and function of retinal circuitry are much less impacted by abnormal visual experience than higher visual areas.
source: For example, although normal visual experience is required for normal topographic maps, orientation selectivity, and direction selectivity in higher visual areas (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Huberman et al., 2008), the structure and function of retinal circuitry are much less impacted by abnormal visual experience (D'Orazi et al., 2014; Elstrott and Feller, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Direction-selective ganglion cells in the retina have mature responses at birth, and they have normal directional tuning, speed tuning, and anatomy in dark-reared animals.
source: Taking the case of direction selectivity as an example, whereas raising animals in the dark prevents the emergence of direction-selective responses in the primary visual cortex (Li et al., 2006; Li et al., 2008), direction-selective ganglion cells in the retina have mature responses at birth, and they have normal directional tuning, speed tuning, and anatomy in dark-reared animals (Elstrott and Feller, 2009; Chan and Chiao, 2008; Elstrott et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on retinal development.

claim: In both insects and vertebrates, experience-independent processes, specified by developmental genetic programs, appear to dominate in determining the structure and function of early stages of sensory processing.
source: Thus, in both insects and vertebrates, experience-independent processes, specified by developmental genetic programs, appear to dominate in determining the structure and function of early stages of sensory processing, with the role of sensory experience becoming more prominent in higher-order stages of processing.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawing on comparative neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The role of sensory experience becomes more prominent in higher-order stages of processing.
source: Thus, in both insects and vertebrates, experience-independent processes, specified by developmental genetic programs, appear to dominate in determining the structure and function of early stages of sensory processing, with the role of sensory experience becoming more prominent in higher-order stages of processing.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawing on comparative neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Neural plasticity, like any form of phenotypic plasticity, comes at a cost.
source: Neural plasticity, like any form of phenotypic plasticity, comes at a cost.
evidence: This is a general theoretical statement about plasticity.

claim: Plasticity at the sensory periphery could be subject to an information acquisition cost, stemming from poor reliability or under-sampling of the stimuli being used to evaluate the statistical structure of the environment.
source: For instance, plasticity at the sensory periphery could be subject to an information acquisition cost, stemming from poor reliability or under-sampling of the stimuli being used to evaluate the statistical structure of the environment.
evidence: This is a speculative theoretical consideration.

claim: Another potential cost of plasticity could arise from temporal mismatching, for instance, if the stimulus structure of the environment were to shift more rapidly than the timescale over which neural plasticity could be implemented.
source: Another potential cost of plasticity could arise from temporal mismatching, for instance, if the stimulus structure of the environment were to shift more rapidly than the timescale over which neural plasticity could be implemented.
evidence: This is a speculative theoretical consideration.

claim: Generating a relatively stable representation of the world at the early stages of processing, which is invariant to local shifts in the stimulus environment, may be the best strategy.
source: Generating a relatively stable representation of the world at the early stages of processing, which is invariant to local shifts in the stimulus environment, maybe the best strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Neural plasticity acting at later stages of processing may allow different downstream circuits to independently reformat the sensory representation in a way that best subserves its specialized function.
source: The initial sensory representation is relayed to multiple higher-order processing areas, each of which may use the sensory information for different behavioral tasks. Neural plasticity acting at later stages of processing may allow different downstream circuits to independently reformat the sensory representation in a way that best subserves its specialized function.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the functional organization of sensory systems.
